titleStmt.title: Telegram From the Department of State to the Embassies in Venezuela, Bolivia, France, Spain, Chile, the United Kingdom, and the Federal Republic of Germany

div.head: 479. Telegram From the Department of State to the Embassies in Venezuela, Bolivia, France, Spain, Chile, the United Kingdom, and the Federal Republic of Germany
div.p: 360395. Subject: Meeting between Secretary and President Lusinchi, December 4, 1984: Chile, Bolivia and Bilateral issues.
1. (C—Entire text).

2. Summary. In addition to Central America and the Caribbean (Guyana, Aruba), Secretary and President Lusinchi discussed a number of bilateral issues as well as Chile and Bolivia. Secretary shared Venezuela’s concern over developments in both these countries. The Secretary had strong praise for Venezuela’s progress on public debt negotiations, urging resolution of the private debt question as well as an improvement in the investment by settlement of the oil nationalization claims. Lusinchi put in a plug to have a Venezuelan replace Ortiz Mena as President of the Inter-American Development Bank.

3. Secretary Shultz called on President Lusinchi during latter’s December 3–5 State visit. Foreign Minister Morales Paul, Minister of the Presidency Consalvi, Finance Minister Azpurua and Ambassador to U.S. Hernandez were with Lusinchi. Ambassador Shlaudeman, Assistant Secretary Motley, Ambassador Landau and ARA/AND Director Rondon accompanied Secretary.
4. Chile.

The Secretary told President Lusinchi that we shared the concerns the Venezuelan President expressed over Chile and Bolivia earlier in the day to President Reagan. In Chile, the Secretary stated that our policy has three objectives: to support a return to democracy, to let Pinochet know privately and publicly that we oppose the recent wave of repression and to encourage the moderate opposition to stay away from the communists. If the moderates align themselves with the extreme left, they will lose the support of moderate elements elsewhere in the world, the Secretary commented. In addition, the Chilean moderates would give Pinochet a handle with which to beat them. The Secretary added that we do not want to see the communists supplant Pinochet. We do want to give Chilean centrists a chance to express their views.
5. Secretary Shultz expressed concern over French and Spanish efforts with the extreme left in Chile.

6. President Lusinchi opined that Chilean Socialists such as Altamirano and Almeyda have little weight. He thought that the centrists are getting stronger in Chile. The Secretary urged that the United States and Venezuela stay in close touch on Chile.
7. Bolivia.

We have provided lots of support for Bolivia, the Secretary stated, but as things stand now the Siles government has to take measures we are able to support. Assistant Secretary Motley noted that American help to Bolivia has run at the rate of about dols 100 million a year. He stressed that the economy is weak in Bolivia and failure to adopt effective economic measures is exacerbating the political situation.
8. Narcotics.

The Secretary welcomed narcotics cooperation between the United States and Venezuela. He pointed to the interest of both the President and Mrs. Reagan in narcotics control. He asked to be kept informed if the United States is not forthcoming in the field of narcotics.
9. IMET.

Secretary Shultz referred to President Lusinchi’s request to President Reagan for a greater American contribution to the IMET program between the United States and Venezuela. The Secretary said we want to be helpful and will double our program this year, from dols 50,000 to dols 100,000.
10. Venezuelan steel.

The Secretary expressed surprise that Venezuela is
concerned over its steel exports to the United States. He commented that Venezuela is a relatively small exporter and its sales have not drawn great attention in the United States, where we are more concerned over steel sales by large producers. Secretary Shultz cautioned, however, that there can be no guarantee that there might not be concern in the future. Lusinchi explained that his government is simply anticipating possible problems.
11. Debt Negotiations.

You must have a genius for a Finance Minister, if you can resolve your debt problems without recourse to the IMF, the Secretary commented. He expressed the hope that Venezuela would be able also to clear up the question of private indebtedness. Lusinchi thanked Shultz for his words of encouragement and the goodwill of the United States.
12. Investment climate: Oil nationalization claims.

The Secretary observed that it is fundamental to get people to invest in Venezuela. In this connection, the Secretary urged resolution of the oil compensation issue. He recalled that he raised this matter with President Lusinchi in Caracas at their breakfast in February. He felt that a settlement would not be very costly for Venezuela and would impact very favorably on investor attitudes. He urged President Lusinchi to work with Ambassador Landau to find a solution.
13. Inter-American Development Bank.

President Lusinchi also put in a plug to have a Venezuela citizen replace Antonio Ortiz Mena as President of the Inter-American Development Bank. The Secretary noted that Ortiz Mena has been retiring for a long time and said the United States would look at a Venezuelan candidate with interest.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D840782–0523. Confidential; Immediate; Exdis. Drafted by Rondon; cleared by Kilday and McKinley and S/S–O, and ARA/SC in draft; approved by Shultz.

In telegram 359904 to multiple diplomatic and consular posts, December 6, the Department reported on the Caribbean issues discussed by Shultz and Lusinchi in their December 4 meeting. (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D840782–0242) A memorandum of conversation for Shultz’s December 4, 4:30 p.m. meeting with Lusinchi on Central America in the Presidential Suite of the Madison Hotel is in the Department of State, Executive Secretariat, S/S Records, 1984 Nodis and Exdis Memorandums, Lot 94D91, Nodis Memorandums, December 1–31, 1984.
